title: The skull's dream
hookLine: Zhuangzi pillows on a skull, which tells him in a dream the dead have no kings and no seasons

cards: A traveler on the road to the state of Chu spots something by the path: a skull, empty, dried out, bleached. The traveler is Zhuangzi, a Daoist thinker whose book often makes serious points through jokes.
He pokes the skull with his riding whip and starts asking it questions. Did you love life too greedily? Were you executed?
Did you do something shameful and die of the disgrace? Did you starve, or freeze? Or did your years simply run out?
Then he pulls the skull over, puts his head on it like a pillow, and goes to sleep.

teach.h: THE SKULL SPEAKS IN A DREAM.
teach.b: In the middle of the night, in chapter eighteen of the Zhuangzi, the skull appears to him in a dream and complains. You talk like a debater, it says. All the things you asked about are troubles of the living.
The dead have none of that.
Among the dead, it says, there's no ruler above and no servant below, and none of the work of the four seasons. Easy and unhurried, with heaven and earth for its springs and autumns.
Even a king on his throne has no happiness greater than this. Zhuangzi doesn't quite believe it.

So he makes an offer: what if I asked the one in charge of life to give you back your bones and flesh and skin, and send you home to your parents, your wife and children, your old friends? And the skull frowns deeply.
Why would I throw away a king's happiness, it asks, to take up the troubles of the living again? End of story.
Some readers take the skull at its word, a picture of death as rest.
Others hear Zhuangzi teasing: a skull lecturing a philosopher, in a dream, about a place no one returns from. The book doesn't settle it, and it seems to enjoy not settling it.
What it does do is take our fear, poke it with a whip, and use it for a pillow.

how: The Zhuangzi is read in Daoist circles and in Chinese literature classes alike; readers return to its death stories, like the skull, for comfort, for argument and for their humor.

o: an emperor who searched all of China for a way to live forever
a Daoist sage who dreamed a skull praised the rest of the dead
the teacher who set the rites for honoring the dead

games.q: who says what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: pokes the skull and asks how it died
speaks in a dream at midnight
no ruler above, no servant below
flesh and bones, and home again

s: the skull is glad to be offered its life back
it frowns deeply and asks why it would give up a king's happiness.
Zhuangzi uses the skull as a pillow and falls asleep
that's how the skull gets to speak: in his dream.
every reader takes the skull's speech as plain teaching about death
some take it at its word; others hear Zhuangzi teasing.

games.q: you're the skull. a philosopher offers to give you back your body and send you home to your family. what do you say?
o: why would I give up a king's happiness for the troubles of the living?
only if I can be a king this time.
games.why: the skull frowns deeply and turns him down. the story ends there, and leaves the reader to decide how seriously to take it.

practice: Rest your head on a pillow, a folded arm or the back of a chair, and let its weight really go into it, noticing how much your neck has been holding all day.
Then let the skull's question come once, without needing an answer: what am I carrying that I'd be glad to set down?

wordCard.voice: Zhuangzi, the Daoist thinker who dreamed a skull told him the dead have no kings and no seasons, and wouldn't trade that for life again. Today's word.

orig.note: Classical Chinese, from the Zhuangzi, a Daoist book: dulou, a skull. Modern Mandarin reading.

carryVoice: Your line: a king's happiness. Whether the skull is joking, the book leaves to you. See you tomorrow.
